warmup.text: Read Carl Sandburg's poem Buffalo Dusk three times before you write anything. Notice which lines are short and which one is very long. This is a benchmark check: name every element you can find.

words.text: Write four comparison sentences today, then match words to their roots and hunt for misspellings. In the game, four new pairs of root words are waiting on the shelf.

reading.text: Today you read three real primary sources from this year: a worker's diary from Sutter's Mill, a reporter's San Francisco, and a Choctaw leader's letter. Choose the one that fits your essay. Then try the Read Like a Writer box.

assignment.text: Your essay has five paragraphs, organized by category. Today write paragraph one, your opening, and paragraph two, your first category, with both novels side by side.

readnow.text: No new chapter today. Read three real primary sources and choose one for your essay.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you work. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Knowing who made a source, and when, tells you what it can prove.
how.use: You will use it in source question 2.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Fixing one kind of mistake at a time catches more of them.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on.
how.why: Thinking first gives you something to watch for.

do: Read the poem out loud three times.
Read the tip.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: Naming every element at work shows you how a poem is built.

do: Read the grammar tools.
Write the four sentences in the box.
Label each one with the tool you used.
how.why: This is your Show What You Know for grammar this week.

do: Find one root word in a source and write about it in your reading journal.
Tap a word, then tap its root.
Match all four.
how.why: Roots work the same way in a novel and in a real diary.

do: Fix the eight words in your reading journal.
Tap every misspelled word in the line.
how.why: Finding mistakes in someone else's writing trains your eye for your own.

do: Read the background card.
Read sources A, B and C.
Answer the three source questions.
how.why: A real voice from the time shows what one real person saw, which a novel cannot.

do: Read the five-paragraph plan.
Write paragraph 1 and paragraph 2 in the box.
Use your claim and categories from Day 1.
how.why: Starting with the opening and one category gets the hardest part done.

cards.title: Real history: who was real?
cards.intro: Every novel this year mixes made-up people with real ones. Here is who really lived.

items.meaning: Kit Tyler, Johnny Tremain, Isaac, Jack Flagg and Praiseworthy are characters the authors invented.
Real. He grew up in Salem, taught himself mathematics and navigation, and in 1802 published The New American Practical Navigator, a book sailors used for more than a hundred years.

items.term: Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, James Otis, Joseph Warren
items.meaning: Real. They were Boston patriots in the 1770s, and all of them appear in Johnny Tremain.
Real. He was a Choctaw leader. In How I Became a Ghost he appears as a ghost who helps the children.
Real. Marshall found gold at Sutter's sawmill on January 24, 1848, the find the miners tell about in Chapter 16 of By the Great Horn Spoon!

cards.note: Sources: the novels themselves; National Park Service and California State Parks; you met Bowditch, Pushmataha and Sutter's Mill on earlier cards.

game.title: Two Books, One Root
game.sub: This week's word game · 4 pairs today
game.look: Five novels and one more book on the shelf: You. Two words with the same root are a pair. Each pair you find ties two worlds together with a gold thread.

do: Tap a card to turn it over.
Tap a second card.
Same root? The pair stays up. Different roots? They turn back over.
how.why: A root is the same in every book. Spotting it lets you read a word you have never seen.

game.miss: Look for the same few letters inside both words.
game.doneLine: Come back next lesson for four new pairs.

pairs.why: Spectral means ghostly, a shape you seem to see; spectators look on, like the crowd at the big fight.
Ships transport gold-seekers; Salem ships carried goods home to import them.
A current is water that runs; a courier runs with messages, as Johnny rides for the patriots. The French spelling of the root is cour.
A tooth extractor pulls teeth; a distraction pulls attention away, like Jumper in the river.

virtue.name: wisdom
virtue.title: Wisdom in the year's books
virtue.intro: Tap the moment from this year's novels that you think shows the most wisdom.

options.t: Praiseworthy talks a crowd out of a hanging with no trial (By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 16).
Nat: “when you depend on a book and it has a mistake, you’d have been safer not depending on it” (Carry On, Mr. Bowditch, Chapter 22).
James Otis: “we fight, we die, for a simple thing. Only that a man can stand up” (Johnny Tremain, Chapter 8).
Isaac, on the very first page: “Be careful what you wish for” (How I Became a Ghost, Chapter 1).

virtue.line: In one sentence: why is this wise?

art.title: A View of Part of the Town of Boston
art.alt: A hand-colored print of Boston seen from the harbor: church steeples and rooftops along the shore, a long wharf, and British warships with small boats carrying soldiers to land.
art.look: Paul Revere engraved this view of British warships landing soldiers at Boston in 1768. This copy was colored and printed again in 1898. Revere is a real person in Johnny Tremain, and this is the harbor and the Long Wharf Johnny knows.
